Pros:
Lowest BOM cost of any Voron printer — compact size means less extrusion, smaller bed, fewer parts
Fully enclosed — prints ABS and ASA reliably in a desktop-friendly package
Faster to build than V2.4 or Trident — lower part count, less cable management
Same Klipper ecosystem as full-size Vorons — config structure and community resources overlap
LDO V0.2 kit is one of the best-value Voron kits available
Description: The Voron 0.2 is the compact fully-enclosed CoreXY in the Voron family — a 120mm build volume printer using 1515 extrusion, built for small functional parts in ABS and ASA where an enclosed chamber matters. It’s the fastest Voron to build and the lowest BOM cost, making it a strong secondary printer or a first Voron for builders who don’t need large volume. The 0.2 revision addressed the front idler issues that plagued the 0.1.
Verdict Label: Best compact enclosed self-build — ABS-capable in a small footprint, lowest Voron BOM cost
Cons:
120×120×120mm build volume — limiting as a primary printer; excellent as a secondary or specialty machine
1515 extrusion requires different hardware than 2020 builds — sourcing is more specialized
Manual bed leveling — no auto-leveling routine; tramming requires attention at build time
Some V0.2 front idler geometry is known to require careful assembly for good belt tension
Name: Voron 0.2

Pros:
Compact enclosed CoreXY design from RatRig — the concept was sound
EVA Mini toolhead and Klipper-native config were part of the broader RatRig ecosystem
Description: The RatRig V-Minion has been discontinued and is no longer supported by RatRig. No active kit is available and official documentation is no longer maintained. Builders looking for a compact enclosed CoreXY with kit support should look at the Voron 0.2 instead — larger community, active LDO kit, and ongoing development.
Verdict Label: Discontinued — RatRig no longer supports the V-Minion; no active kit, no official documentation updates
Cons:
No longer supported by RatRig — no active kit, no documentation updates, no official community support
Choose Voron 0.2 instead: larger community, active development, LDO kit available
Sourcing parts requires finding discontinued components; not recommended for a new build
Name: RatRig V-Minion

Pros:
AWD motion uses 4 independent XY stepper motors — eliminates belt tension asymmetry and simplifies high-acceleration tuning
3030 aluminum extrusion frame is substantially more rigid than 2020 — less frame flex at high print speeds
Official RatRig kit with documentation, support, and a structured build guide — more scaffolding than pure Voron community builds
EVA 3 toolhead supports multiple hotends with standardized mounting
Klipper native with an official RatRig configuration maintained by the company
Description: The RatRig V-Core 4 is the premier commercially-kitted self-build CoreXY, distinguished by its All-Wheel-Drive (AWD) 4-motor XY motion and 3030 aluminum extrusion frame. Available in 300mm, 400mm, and 500mm build volumes; price scales with size. AWD eliminates conventional belt tension asymmetry and the 3030 frame is meaningfully stiffer than Voron’s 2020 baseline. Official RatRig documentation and community support is the key differentiator from pure-community Voron builds.
Verdict Label: Best-supported self-build kit — AWD CoreXY, 3030 frame rigidity, official documentation and RatRig community backing
Cons:
AWD requires 4 stepper drivers for XY — mainboard or toolboard planning is more complex than standard 2-motor CoreXY
Kit cost is higher than self-sourcing equivalent Voron parts
EVA 3 toolhead has less community modding depth than Stealthburner
3030 extrusion costs more and weighs more than 2020 — shipping weight and parts cost increase with build size
Name: RatRig V-Core 4

Pros:
300mm build volume handles the vast majority of functional parts without the cost and weight of a 350mm build
Same QGL, Tap, and Stealthburner ecosystem as all V2.4 sizes
The most-built V2.4 variant — more community build logs, tuning guides, and mod documentation exist for the 300 than any other size
Best balance of BOM cost and build area in the V2.4 lineup
Description: The Voron 2.4 is the benchmark CoreXY self-build — a fully enclosed flying-gantry printer where 4 independent Z motors tram the gantry (not the bed) via Quad Gantry Level. Available in 250mm, 300mm, and 350mm build volumes; the 300mm is the community sweet spot. Klipper is the sole supported firmware; the official config and documentation on vorondesign.com are the most comprehensive in any self-build community.
Verdict Label: Best-documented self-build in existence — deepest community, config library, and mod ecosystem of any open-source printer
Cons:
4 Z motors and QGL still requires careful commissioning — same complexity as 250mm and 350mm
Slightly heavier and more expensive than 250mm; still less capable than 350mm if volume is the priority
Not a short build — same time investment as all V2.4 variants
Name: Voron 2.4

Pros:
300mm Z volume matches X and Y — the Trident 300 is more cubic than the V2.4 300 (which loses Z to gantry clearance)
3-point lead screw Z is faster to commission and easier to diagnose than QGL
Same Stealthburner, Tap, and Klipper ecosystem as all Voron printers
Full Voron community behind it
Description: The Voron Trident uses a moving-bed Z mechanism — 3 independent lead screws under the bed tram the surface via 3-point auto-leveling, while the gantry is fixed in Z. Available in 250mm, 300mm, and 350mm; the 300mm variant is the most common choice and delivers a fully cubic build volume. XY motion, Stealthburner toolhead, and Klipper ecosystem are identical to the V2.4.
Verdict Label: Simpler Z than the V2.4, same Voron toolchain — the better first Voron for builders who don’t need flying-gantry complexity
Cons:
Moving bed in Z can affect print stability on extremely tall parts
Slightly less active mod development than V2.4 in some edge areas
Same build complexity and time commitment as V2.4 in XY
Name: Voron Trident

Pros:
Lowest entry cost if you already own an Ender 3 — BOM is primarily new motion parts
Brings Klipper and CoreXZ motion to an existing bed-slinger platform
Full Voron mod ecosystem access
Smaller and faster to build than a V2.4 or Trident from scratch
Description: The Voron Switchwire is a legacy design — a CoreXZ motion conversion for the Ender 3 platform that Voron has largely moved on from. It reuses the donor printer’s frame and Y-axis while replacing XZ motion with CoreXZ belts. The concept made sense when it launched; in 2024–2025, the V0.2 has made it largely redundant. It remains in the Voron project but receives minimal development attention and has the smallest, least-active community of any current Voron design.
Verdict Label: Legacy design — Voron considers this superseded; only worth pursuing if you already own an Ender 3 and have a specific reason not to build a V0.2 instead
Cons:
Requires a donor Ender 3, Ender 3 Pro, or Ender 3 V2 — cost from scratch is not competitive
CoreXZ motion means the toolhead moves in both X and Z — heavier toolhead mass limits speed more than CoreXY
Legacy design — Voron has moved on; this is the least active Voron variant with minimal recent development
If you own an Ender 3 and want to upgrade, a Trident or V0.2 new build is a better use of budget than this conversion
No active mod momentum — most community energy has been on V2.4, Trident, and V0.2 for years
Name: Voron Switchwire

Pros:
Speed-optimized from the ground up — gantry geometry and moving mass decisions are engineered for high-acceleration Klipper printing, not retrofitted
Goliath hotend integrates natively with the VzBot toolhead — high-flow performance in the same package
Klipper Input Shaper documentation and resonance tuning resources are deeply embedded in the VzBot community
Open source — all design files on GitHub
Active Discord community of expert-level contributors
Description: The VzBot is an open-source CoreXY designed from the ground up for high-acceleration Klipper printing. Available in 235mm and 330mm build volumes; the 235mm is the more common starting point. Every gantry geometry decision — reduced moving mass, stiffened XY motion, toolhead weight minimization — exists to push Input Shaper resonance peaks higher. Expert-only territory: rewards builders who already know Klipper inside out.
Verdict Label: Highest acceleration potential of any printer in this guide — speed-optimized design from the ground up, expert-only build territory
Cons:
Not beginner territory — assumes Klipper fluency, Input Shaper experience, and mechanical debugging comfort
Smaller community than Voron — fewer mods, fewer people to debug with when something goes wrong
Sourcing some VzBot-specific parts requires more research than Voron’s well-established vendor network
Not enclosed by default — ABS printing requires an enclosure add-on
High complexity overhead: if you’re not running high-speed printing, the build doesn’t justify itself
Name: VzBot

Pros:
Parallel Z lifting mechanism with high-quality lead screws delivers exceptional Z repeatability — dimensional accuracy is the design goal
Kinematic bed mounts (standard in most HevORT builds) minimize first-layer variance over time
Fully enclosed — chamber temperature stability supported by default design
Klipper native; community configs exist on GitHub
Open source — all design files accessible for builders who want to customize extensively
Description: The HevORT HRE (High Resolution Enclosure) is a self-build CoreXY designed around dimensional precision and Z-axis repeatability. Available in a standard 300mm configuration and a larger 400mm+ variant; the design is highly configurable. The parallel Z lifting system and magnetic kinematic bed mounts minimize first-layer error over time. The community is small and primarily European; parts sourcing and build support require more self-sufficiency than Voron or RatRig builds.
Verdict Label: Precision-first self-build with the best Z repeatability in this guide — expert only, smallest community, no kit
Cons:
Smallest community in this guide — much harder to find active troubleshooting help, build logs, or config examples outside the core HevORT Discord
No official kit — all parts are self-sourced; vendors are often European with longer shipping times to North America
Documentation gaps exist — some build areas require reading GitHub issues or Discord history directly
Not a good first self-build; assumes significant mechanical and Klipper experience
Low brand recognition limits resale value and second-hand trading
Name: HevORT HRE
